"Spoil" means to damage or ruin something — to take something that was good and make it worse, or even completely useless. Think of it as a word for when something goes from a good state to a bad one. That is the thread that connects almost every use of this word.

1. To Ruin an Experience or a Moment

This is the most everyday use. When something spoils an experience, it takes away the joy or pleasure from it.

The heavy rain spoiled our picnic.
His rude comment spoiled the entire evening.
Don't let one bad moment spoil your whole day.

Notice that the thing doesn't have to be physically destroyed. A moment, a mood, a celebration — all of these can be spoiled. The damage is to the quality of the experience.

2. To Ruin Food (by Going Bad)

When food spoils, it goes bad — it becomes unsafe or unpleasant to eat. This is a very natural and common use.

Milk spoils quickly if you leave it out of the fridge.
The meat had spoiled by the time we got home.
Store it properly, or it will spoil.

Here, "spoil" is often used without an object — the food spoils on its own. You don't need anyone to cause it; it just happens.

3. To Ruin a Surprise or a Story (a "Spoiler")

When someone spoils a story, a movie, or a surprise, they reveal information that was meant to be a secret — especially an ending or a twist — before the other person gets to discover it themselves.

Please don't spoil the movie for me. I haven't seen it yet.
He spoiled the surprise party by telling her in advance.
I accidentally spoiled the book's ending for my friend.

This is where the popular word "spoiler" comes from — a spoiler is a piece of information that spoils your experience of discovering something for yourself.

4. To Treat Someone Too Generously (Often a Child)

When you spoil a person — especially a child — you give them too much of what they want. You fulfill every wish, never say no, and shield them from disappointment. Over time, this can lead to the person becoming selfish, demanding, or unable to handle not getting what they want.

Her grandparents spoil her with sweets and gifts every visit.
He was spoiled as a child, and now he expects everything to go his way.
Stop spoiling him — he needs to learn that he can't always have everything.

This meaning carries a slightly negative tone — to spoil someone this way is generally seen as doing them a disservice, even if the intention is love.

However, in a lighter, warmer context, you can also use "spoil" to mean treating someone very well — not necessarily to excess, but generously and lovingly.

Let me spoil you tonight — dinner is on me.
She spoiled her guests with a luxurious three-course meal.

In this softer sense, it's a compliment. The context will always tell you which meaning is intended.

5. To Deliberately Ruin a Ballot Paper

In the context of voting, to spoil a ballot means to mark it in a way that makes it invalid and uncountable — either intentionally, as a form of protest, or by accident.

He chose to spoil his ballot rather than vote for any of the candidates.
A number of votes were spoiled due to unclear markings.

To spoil someone rotten — to spoil someone to an extreme degree.

Those grandparents spoil that child rotten.

To be spoiled for choice — to have so many good options that it's hard to choose. (This is a positive expression.)

With so many great restaurants in the city, we were spoiled for choice.

To spoil the fun — to ruin an enjoyable situation, often by being overly serious or strict.

Don't be a killjoy and spoil the fun.

To spoil the party — similar to above; to disrupt something pleasant.

She arrived late and spoiled the party with her bad mood.
An Important Nuance: Who Does the Ruining?

One beautiful thing about "spoil" is its flexibility in terms of cause.

  • A person can spoil something: He spoiled the ending.
  • A thing or situation can spoil something: The weather spoiled the trip.
  • Something can spoil on its own, with no outside cause: The food spoiled overnight.

All three patterns are natural and correct.

Even though "spoil" has several meanings, they all share one idea: something goes from a good or intended state to a worse one. Food was fresh — now it's rotten. A surprise was intact — now it's ruined. A child was balanced — now they're overindulged. A moment was joyful — now it's been damaged.

Once you hold onto that core idea, every use of "spoil" will make instant sense to you.
